chunks: As for what was narrated by Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, from Sayf, from Yūnus, from the one who narrated it, he said:

Ṭawāf al-nisāʾ is only upon the pilgrim performing hajj. So this does not conflict with what we have mentioned, because this narration is mawqūf, not musnad to any of the Imams عليهم السلام. When it is not musnad, acting upon it is not obligatory, because it is possible that this was a view of Yūnus which he chose according to some of his opinions, just as he chose many views to which we are not bound to adhere, due to the establishment of proof for their invalidity.

key_terms.الدَّلَالَةِ: the evidentiary indication establishing a ruling or judgment
key_terms.الْأَئِمَّةِ: the Imams, the authoritative transmitters and guides in Shia tradition
key_terms.طَوَافُ النِّسَاءِ: the circumambulation required in pilgrimage rites relating to marital permissibility
key_terms.مَذْهَبًا: a juristic view or doctrinal position adopted by a narrator
key_terms.مَوْقُوفَةٌ: a report halted at a narrator and not elevated to an Imam عليه السلام
key_terms.مُسْنَدَةٍ: fully attributed through sanad/isnad to an authoritative source

ai.seo_question: Why is an unconnected hadith about Ṭawāf al-nisāʾ not considered binding in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This passage discusses a legal report about Ṭawāf al-nisāʾ and argues that it cannot override established rulings because it is not fully attributed to any of the Imams عليهم السلام. It highlights the importance of sanad/isnad evaluation in determining whether a report is binding in jurisprudence.
